awd_titl_txt: EA: Acquisition of a Terrestrial Laser Scanner for Student Engagement and Research on Critical Zone Processes
awd_abstract_narration:
This project will acquire a terrestrial laser scanner (TLS). The TLS is a portable device that captures detailed 3D images of the ground, vegetation and other landscape features, and buildings. These precise, high-quality data will support advanced studies in Earth Sciences and related fields. TLS images are used to model surfaces, observe natural processes, and create high-resolution maps. The new TLS will empower students at Boise State University to address pressing environmental issues. These include understanding carbon storage and loss and the effects of climate change on water resources. Students will gain experience in data science and field data collection, applicable to many career paths. Additionally, the TLS will foster student teamwork, through collaborative studies on diverse research topics.

The Department of Geosciences at Boise State University will receive the Riegl VZ-600i TLS and its accompanying software and training. The TLS will be available for research and education across the department and with its partners. It will be used primarily to characterize organic and inorganic carbon budgets in western U.S. drylands (rangelands). The TLS will enhance graduate student projects in quantifying changes in peatland carbon, including studies on peatland microtopography and vegetation from elevated CO2 and temperature experiments. It will also support advanced studies in hydrology, ecohydrology, and geomorphology, while driving innovation in models of ecohydrology and erosion. Finally, the TLS will play a pivotal role in engaging the broader community. Undergraduate and graduate students will gain hands-on experience with this cutting-edge technology, sharpening their analytical and critical thinking skills. Through outreach programs, K-12 students will interact with it, promoting Earth Science and related careers to a new generation. With its mobility and ease of use, the new TLS will be a vital asset for addressing national research priorities, building education and research capacity, and fostering a deeper understanding of our planet’s dynamic systems across academic and public audiences.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This project supported the acquisition and deployment of a Riegl VZ-600i terrestrial laser scanner (TLS) for research and education in the Department of Geosciences at Boise State University. A terrestrial laser scanner is a portable instrument that rapidly collects millions of highly accurate three-dimensional measurements of the ground surface, vegetation, and built environments. These data allow researchers and students to create detailed digital models of landscapes and better understand environmental change.

The TLS was used to advance research in Earth and environmental sciences, particularly studies focused on ecosystem change, carbon cycling, vegetation structure, hydrology, and geomorphic processes. Researchers and students used the instrument to quantify changes in peatland surfaces exposed to elevated carbon dioxide and warming experiments and to evaluate how these changes influenced microtopography (surface features) and tree growth. The scanner was also used to document vegetation structure and environmental conditions at long-term monitoring locations within the Reynolds Creek Experimental Watershed, a nationally recognized research site managed by the USDA Agricultural Research Service. This work is being used to improve historic snow monitoring datasets by measuring vegetation growth to contextualize canopy impacts on snow accumulation, which will advance future snow modeling and downstream water availability calculations. 

The project also supported rapid-response field research following wildfire-related debris flow events associated with an National Science Foundation RAPID award. High-resolution 3D data collected with the TLS improved the ability of researchers to characterize post-fire erosion and landscape response. In addition to research applications, the TLS contributed to interdisciplinary outreach activities. Boise State University students used the instrument in collaboration with the Idaho State Police during cold-case investigations, combining terrestrial laser scanning with ground-penetrating radar to support forensic searches.

A major outcome of the project was the training and development of undergraduate and graduate students in advanced geospatial science and remote sensing methods. Students gained hands-on experience operating the TLS in field environments, processing large 3D datasets, registering data to GPS coordinates, and analyzing point clouds to extract information about landscapes and vegetation. These activities provided training in geospatial analysis, field methods, teamwork, and scientific data management that are directly relevant to careers in Earth science, environmental monitoring, engineering, and related technical fields.

The project strengthened Boise State University’s research infrastructure by providing a modern and mobile terrestrial laser scanner that could be shared across research groups and educational activities. The instrument increased opportunities for collaboration among university researchers, federal agencies, and community partners while supporting broader participation in Earth science and geospatial technologies. Through demonstrations, field activities, and outreach events, the project also introduced students and collaborators to advanced environmental imaging technologies and their applications for understanding natural systems and addressing real-world environmental challenges.

Overall, the project expanded research and educational capacity in geospatial science, improved access to advanced remote sensing technologies, and contributed to a better understanding of dynamic environmental processes of our Earth.
